review_text_raw:
If you're only just now hearing about Simulacra because it got a sequel, don't feel bad... you're not alone. Somehow this sci-fi horror simulation game ended up flying under the radar of a lot of people until recently. It comes from Kaigan Games, the creators of Sarah Is Missing; a title unavailable on Steam, but is playable for free over on Itch.io. It's a very similar predecessor to Simulacra, and perhaps it helped to serve as an unrefined beta for this more solid-feeling experience.

To say much about the story is to give away the entire game, so to give a very brief synopsis... you found a phone on your doorstep. Opening and accessing its apps leads you to discover that it was previously owned by a girl named Anna. After some digging around in the contents of the device and chatting with her boyfriend and best friend, you realize that Anna has gone missing, and she has been missing for some time. You'll have to recover data, browse photos and videos, and consult with others who were in touch with Anna before her disappearance in order to try and figure out what happened to her, and if you're capable of finding her and saving her life.

The entire game centers around Anna's phone; there's never a time where you will not be using it. The developers have done an outstanding job with creating an entire, believable world within the device; it's fabulously easy to slip into the realm of Simulacra and lose hours of time just checking out all of the dating profiles, work e-mails, and off-beat articles that were added to make the game just that much more realistic. There are several of these websites and news articles to read through, handfuls of in-depth e-mails, tons of selfies of Anna that show off her life and interests, and apps that simulate ones that most of us have installed on our own phones. Of course, a lot of these things are essential components to solving little detective-style puzzles, but there's also a good portion that is just there for entertainment. The game feels like an expansive ARG (alternate reality game), and if one were to play this title on an actual mobile device then the immersion would be surreal.

There are very few areas here that need any work, but the voice acting is one of them. A lot of the voice-overs, especially for Anna's boyfriend, are just embarrassingly cringe-worthy. The acting seen in many of the videos is also pretty bad, but not as bad as the voice work. Those are the only real complaints here, and they're honestly just nitpicky as they can be overlooked with ease. The game's interface is user-friendly, there's a great speed up option unlocked after beating the story once so that players can quickly get to the other four endings (as there are five) and explore different dialogue options, and there's enough small little horror elements to keep the gameplay tense throughout the first playthrough. Overall, it's one of the best casual, story-based sci-fi horror experiences out there right now.

Simulacra is one of those rare gems that manages to slip under the radar of most people; despite being out for almost three years and having over 1,000 reviews on Steam. It's the perfect blend of technology-based sci-fi and subtle horror, in the same vein of TV shows like Black Mirror and Dark Net. While its premise might sound cheesy, this title has some of the most immersive content that I've ever personally witnessed in the thousands of games that I've played. It borders on being an ARG, as there is an incredible level of attention to detail within every app, website, and chat that you'll delve into. Though an initial playthrough only takes about four hours, that time will be sucked away and you'll be left wondering how the hell it got so late, so fast. You'll also be left craving more, so definitely check out Sarah Is Missing and Simulacra 2 afterwards.

[b]Last time I pick up a random phone.[/b]

One day, you find a phone just sitting on your doorstep. Like anybody else, you decide to snoop through the phone either to figure out who the owner is so you can return it or just because you can. However, this turns into a much more complicated situation. The first tip off is that while you are blocked by a lock screen, the phone glitches so you can get into it. I don’t know about anybody else, but I wouldn’t have looked through it after that. Anyway, you soon find out that the phone’s owner is Anna and she has recently gone missing. Thus, you decide to look through her phone activity and talk to her friends and acquaintances in an attempt to find her before it’s too late.

There are some puzzles here with the most frequent puzzle you’ll come across involves unscrambling text messages and photos. For texts, you’ll have to order the words in the right order. Photos are more complicated as you’re given several fragments to piece together, but you can’t have any part that is glitched. So you’ll have to figure out which order will allow all glitched out parts to be replaced with the picture. The other puzzle you’ll come across involve you gathering information through either the sites Anna frequented or through her friends. The only problem I had was that some messages had more than one way that it could make sense and that there is an instance where you’re expected to remember certain facts since you can’t go and look for the information.

The acting is average, with Anna’s actress being the stand out, with hilariously bad parts (aka all of Greg’s voice lines) sprinkled in. Voice acting mainly comes through Anna’s vlogs, audio text messages, and phone calls. What doesn’t exactly make sense are the phone calls. At certain points in the story, you’ll get a phone call from one of the characters and you’ll have to answer it (or they’ll keep calling/story won’t continue). Of course, you can’t answer back and when that character asks why you don’t talk back, the excuse is that you can’t make out what they’re saying (despite you being able to hear them fine). I’d rather have the excuse either be that you guess the mic got broken before you found it (which can also imply that whatever is making the phone glitch is causing the mic to stop working) or it auto sends them to voicemail. [spoiler]It doesn’t make sense even more when a police officer actually calls you but assume he’s leaving a voicemail despite not hearing “leave a message after the beep”.[/spoiler]

[spoiler]Also, I just couldn’t help but laugh at the look she gives Taylor in the ending where both of them live.[/spoiler]

Simulacra has four endings each with their own requirements. While you can’t jump to a specific section of the game, you’ll be able to speed things up on your next playthroughs through Begin+. It won’t take long to build up the requirements you need, but the last sequence plays at the same speed.

While Simulacra isn’t perfect, it’s still worth it to experience it yourself, whether it be on PC or on your phone to get the maximum immersion you can. I did find the phone aspect convincing for the most part, didn’t mind that glitches were used to freak you out (though others might not like it), and liked how they filled in the empty space with a room with ambient noises chiming in. There are even some subtle moments here, like the phone’s background changing. The only thing that really messes with immersion is some of the voice acting.

review_text_raw:
Although this hasn't dethroned The Black Watchmen for the title of my favorite alternate reality game, SIMULACRA is worth a play for anyone who's looking for something spooky, casual, immersive, and a bit of a brainteaser. The price point can't be beat, though I will say that I suspect that playing the appstore version on your phone would probably be more immersive than playing it over Steam.

The story starts with you finding a phone belonging to an attractive girl named Anna. You're allowed to navigate through her email account, her texts, her pics/vids, and various social media accounts, and you quickly figure out that something is seriously amiss. As you contact her friends, ex-boyfriend and other acquaintances you understand that your role as the player is to do quite a lot of snooping and social engineering to uncover whatever happened to Anna. Your choices are saved throughtout the play and shape the ultimate outcome of the story - I believe there are 4 different endings.

You do need to play it a bit smart; at points you will need to obtain access to accounts and people that are not obvious, which may require you to dig deeper into photos and media feeds to discover the information you need. I did not find any of the 'puzzles' overly difficult, but a few did give me some pause while I dug up the information needed to continue.

There is both live acting and voice acting throughout the game, so you definitely need your sound on to play. Some of the voice acting seems very forced (and some voice actors in particular are rather annoying to listen to) but the pics and vids felt real enough and the chats you have with other characters did a good job of giving each one a solid personality.

There is a horror element to the story, but I did not see any overt gore or violence from my own playthrough. There is something of a jumpscare towards the end, but nothing too bad. Lots of Exorcist style demon-grumbling, static, spooky messages and so on to set the mood as you go.

So overall, for the price, it's a worthwhile buy if this type of game appeals to you.

review_text_raw:
Simulacra is an interesting horror game where the events unfold through a phone screen.

Story:

You play as an unnamed man/woman. We find a phone that belongs to a woman named Anna, we find a message of her begging for help and well we launch into an investigation to figure out how to save her.

The story in Simulacra is quite intriguing and all the research you do to figure out what happened to Anna and all the people around her, is quite interesting, because you go through many sites, reading articles and text messages, most of it having some decent writing behind it.

Graphics:

Well the only graphics in this is your phone. The phone has it's own OS named Iris and it's styled after an android phone. It looks quite convincing. You definitely know what each app represents so the art team definitely nailed the look of a smart phone.

Audio:

The acting is pretty sub-par, the actress that plays Anna is the only one that is semi-decent, but everyone else does a pretty mediocre job. However where the game shines the most is in it's audio design. The noises you hear around you when you browse the phone send a shiver down your spine. It could be something simple, like a small whisper to a creepy silent laugh. 

Gameplay:

Simulacra is mostly a puzzle solving game, where you have goals and you have to figure out how solve and these puzzles have a pretty decent design. A liked quite a few of the puzzles and how fresh they felt.

These puzzles range from pretty simple to sometimes head scratching. But it never felt cryptic and actually quite a few of the puzzles required a really logical solution and it felt like it would be something I would do in real life. 

You can do a bunch of research by reading articles, reading text messages so there's a lot of stuff to do in the phone. Also not to mention there's multiple choices throughout the story and multiple endings for you to achieve. 

Verdict:

Simulacra is a pretty unique horror game and it's story is pretty intriguing. With multiple endings and a really interesting plot I loved my time with this game and honestly I suggest giving it a shot at full price.

Pros:
+ Story is pretty intriguing
+ Nails the look of a smartphone perfectly
+ Multiple choices lead to different outcomes and endings
+ Great puzzles

Cons:
- Acting is not good whatsoever 

Final Rating:
8.5/10

review_text_raw:
Picture this: you find a girl's phone, and her name is Anna. But here's the catch - she's missing, and you're the one holding her phone with all its personal information. Creepy, right?

The story revolves around investigating Anna's disappearance, and as you interact with her friends and family through text messages and phone conversations, the tension keeps building up. The drama feels real, and the game's decision-based mechanics force you to make choices that affect the outcome. The best part is, it's not just a mystery unraveling over time; your main goal is clear - find Anna. But beware, Simulacra is not just about jumpscares; it plays with your senses more subtly, with eerie audio effects that might even make you question reality outside the game.

Though the game is quite engaging, it's not without its flaws. The voice acting feels a bit awkward and scripted, and some audio elements seem unnecessary, primarily existing for the sake of providing a jumpscare. But hey, the recorded videos are well done, especially Anna's personal vlogs.

Playing this game on PC might not be as immersive as on a mobile phone but it holds its merit reguardless. Still, they could've allowed portrait mode like in Downwell to make it even better.

All in all, Simulacra is a decent horror title that excels in subtle horror and decision-based gameplay. It really makes you think about privacy, honesty, and data security, and that's something you don't often get from a horror game. So, if you're up for an unnerving experience that's a bit different from the usual horror games, give Simulacra a try!

[h1]A First Impression Review[/h1]

I shouldn't have liked this, but I did. I'm not a horror fan, but the concept was interesting enough to keep me hooked. It reminds me of the movie [i]Smile[/i]. It’s creepy and has some jumpscares that make you feel uncomfortable, but the intrigue of the puzzles actually sold me, despite not being a puzzle guy.

[h1]The Good[/h1]
- [b]Realistic Interface:[/b] Feels exactly like operating a normal Android phone. It's natural and easy to navigate.
- [b]Clever Puzzles:[/b] The difficulty is just right. You have to really think, like hunting through emails to find a mother’s maiden name for a password reset. 
- [b]The Drama:[/b] There is a good chunk of backstory in the messages. Reading through the texts, like the drama with the mom, felt realistic and wild. It adds weight to the mystery. It actually made me care about the missing women. 
- [b]Great Price:[/b] This game is cheap. It's under $10 at full price, and catching it on sale for under $2 is a big W.
- [b]Good Pacing:[/b] The game pushes you in the right direction. If you finish a task, you’ll get an alert letting you know exactly which app or person to investigate next.

[h1]The Not-So-Good[/h1]
- [b]Awkward Acting:[/b] The acting is a little awkward at times. I definitely laughed at a few moments, but it gets the job done and sells the story.

[b]TLDR:[/b] A neat mystery that makes you want to keep playing to see what happens next. If you like unique puzzles and can handle a bit of a creep factor, it’s worth it.

[b]Verdict:[/b]
☐ Skip It
☐ Buy it on Sale
☑️ Worth it at Full Price

There's a sub-genre of games that I like to call voyeur sims -- these include walking simulators like Gone Home, strategy-puzzlers like the Orwell games, and story-driven phone-sim games like [b]SIMULACRA[/b].

These voyeur sims fuel something visceral in me by allowing me to be a peeping tom in someone else's life; overcoming personal privacy as a game mechanic is somehow uncomfortably fun, even when the actual gameplay is minimal.

[b]SIMULACRA[/b] is one of the better voyeur sims and one of the better games I've played this year. Like other phone-sim games like [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/523210/A_Normal_Lost_Phone/]A Normal Lost Phone[/url] and [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/496890/Replica/]Replica[/url], it starts with a mysterious cell phone, and throughout the game, you unpack its content in a series of puzzle-driven unlocking sequences.

What sets [b]SIMULACRA[/b] apart is its high production value. High quality FMVs, passable and explorable versions of popular social media apps, realistic text logs and emails -- these all make the small, contained world of [b]SIMULACRA[/b] believable and immersive.

This is a great game. Recommended.

A supernatural horror story where you use a missing person's phone (texting contacts/viewing photos/reading e-mail/other apps or social media) to figure out what happened to them. Not the same but it gives a similar feel to me as a game like Orwell.

I don't really enjoy horror games in general so I preferred playing this game as a mystery. I didn't really care for the random 'horror' sound effects or imagery. I was a bit disappointed when the plot went for [spoiler]the sci-fi twist. It's alright but I would have liked a regular, more realistic thing. It felt like something outside of your control with no real foreshadowing or buildup. There is nothing to suggest that it was possible and even after you learn about it you can't go back and see much in a new light. It might be nice if they at least put something random about the dangers of AI or something.[/spoiler]

Aside from the general phone-searching there are some minigames. They aren't too tough but one might be harder if you're not a native english speaker. One minigame is taking a jumbled list of words and making the right sentence out of it. However, it's not enough to get an equivalent meaning- you have to get the word order exactly right. For example, 'Meet me and I'll show ya this weekend' is wrong but 'Meet me this weekend and I'll show ya' is right.

Worth a look if you're fine with learning about the missing person story through phone history and dialogue.

Other thoughts:[list]
[*] It's a little annoying that in order to get the 'good' ending you have to [spoiler]manipulate people because there's no way to convince them otherwise.[/spoiler]
[*] I would have liked multiple save slots.
[*] It's nice that it can be set to automatically skip text on repeat playthroughs.
[*] Pretty much no settings to adjust (only subtitles). I would've liked at least volume and resolution options.
[*] Some inconsistencies/strange things: [spoiler]She met Taylor on Spark but had been following him on Jabbr 3 months ago. Cassie's AMA from 3 months ago is still continuing even though it closed (you get to ask a question)? The article mentions a back-and-forth between genders but you're forced to repeat the female gender and use one of the three pre-selected photos (it seems like other pictures don't progress the story). Why is it assimilating the 'weak'? From what I understand it's somehow taking control of a person and building a world out of their simulacrum (online personification?)? And then discarding the physical body for some reason because they can only lure in one person on Spark before they're useless?[/spoiler]
[*] A bunch of grammar and spelling errors and incorrect subtitles.
[*] Only crashed randomly once.
[/list]

Okay, so i just finished playing this (took me something like 5 or 6 hours I believe), and I felt compelled to review this game because it's like nothing I've played before. I had never heard of the "found-phone" genre in games before.

First let me say this: if you're a fan of mysteries, riddles, horror, or to be more specific, found-footage horror, then this game is for you! If not, try it anyway lol you just might be surprised.

This game starts out with you booting up a phone that was sent to you (or left on your doorstep, it's not totally cleared up in the story), and when you do it begins to glitch out a little and then these texts start coming in, and well, it just takes off from there...

The basic premise is that the owner of the phone, a girl named Anna, has gone missing and it's up to you (and a couple others along the way) to try to find her. You do this by digging through her phone and reading EVERYTHING, and then communicating with some of her contacts through texts and emails and an online dating app and a twitter-like app.  As things progress you learn that she has dissapeared and it may be connected to other recent dissapearances (but I won't go into more on that because I don't want to ruin the experience for new players).  Eventually, you realize there's a lot more going on than meets the eye.

The game has a very unnerving, intense feeling to it, and is all the better for it.  It has a decent story, some fun little mini games and riddles, a good amount of investigation and some pretty convinging dialogues, and for the REALLY hardcore sleuths out there, it even has some very interesting "easter eggs" hidden in the game that are quite rewarding to find. (I'll give you a hint here, but that's it...morse code, click it :)   )

As for graphics, sound, story, gameplay, etc...well graphics aren't important here as it's basically a phone emulator, the gameplay is as simple as digging through a phone and talking to people and looking stuff up (but you need a brain lol), the story is interesting enough that you really will never get bored in a single playthrough, and apparently it has many different endings so it has replayability there...where this game really shines though is the sound...it's incredible and really really well done.  When you start they recommend you use headphones, and I STRONGLY recommend you take their advice, it's just not the same on speakers, not even close

Anyway, the TL;DR is this:
if you 're looking for an action title, look elsewhere, but if you're looking for an EXPERIENCE that really makes you feel like you're a part of a mystery that needs to be solved, I can't recommend this highly enough. It's fun as hell!

For me it's a 4.5/5

For full transparency: I got this game in a Humble bundle worth 0.99 cents along with 1 other game.

[b][u]The good[/u][/b]
This game has an engaging story, I was seriously invested in the characters and how this was gonna play out. The characters really had a personality to them. The performance of the person playing Anna in particular was great! 
I liked the piecing together aspect this game had and how you slowly uncover more. It managed to hold my attention, for sure. It took me on a ride that I really enjoyed.
You can see that there was a lot of time and effort put into this game, with all the different things that are on the phone and all the conversations that play out. The little image and word puzzles were a nice touch, too. The game looks good and for the most part sounds good, too. 


[b][u]The bad[/u][/b]
The big reveal at the end of the game was… meh. The mystery to the game was much more fun than the answer to that mystery. Although I did like the endings themselves and their ambiguity.  
There were some repeated grammar mistakes that took me out of the experience. Yes, it’s texting, but I feel like in texting you get more typos and less grammar mistakes. The game would benefit from fixing some of these.
The voice acting was a bit spotty. Some actors did a good job, like the detective or Taylor. However, there was one audio clip of Ashley that felt immersion-breaking to me, and Greg in general didn’t sound good to me at all, it was way over the top.

[b]I encountered a game-breaking bug.[/b] For some reason, if you go in the web browser and go to the history section, all web pages that you should only be supposed to look at later in the game are already available. If you read these, events will trigger and the game will think you’re already at those points. The game then runs both the conversations you were already having and the “new” conversations which completely breaks your savefile. So, until this bug is fixed, [b]don’t look at anything in the history section of the web browser[/b].

[b]TL;DR Nice game, I definitely recommend it! But beware of the bug I talked about ^[/b]

I'm going to divide this review into various sections based on gameplay elements, in a slightly illogical order. This seems appropriate for a slightly illogical game. Also, I ran out of characters, so I had to leave a lot out.

[h2] Sound Design [/h2]
Best part of the game. Only thing that makes it scary.

Even for someone who had quite a few scares spoiled for me due to watching previous playthrough snippits and common internet knowledge, the scares still all GOT ME. And, I mean, they GOT ME. I was jumping in my seat and looking around for the voices I was hearing. At one point [spoiler] I heard a door knocking and thought someone was trying to break into my bedroom [/spoiler]. Those sounds that play, whether phone ringing or human breathing or that terrible [spoiler] wood knocking [/spoiler], were still enough to make me jump after four straight playthroughs. In this game you find a phone that is clearly possessed, and are tasked to find its owner, Anna. You are helped and hindered by the various people trying to get ahold of her, and you can either leave her life in shambles for her to return to or make her life better with your interference.

Dating apps bad. Something about valuing the real world over the virtual. Game certainly doesn't punish you much for becoming a master online troll catfishing manipulator. But maybe...maybe that's the real point. We can look back at a preinternet time and recognize that certain things were better back then. But the fact of the matter is, that world doesn't exist anymore. 

Wow. That went deeper than I thought. Too bad the villian sucks and I don't care about Anna.

Yes. I do.

I think it's fun. Fun like watching the Scream franchise. Fun like a haunted hayride sponsored by a high school, where you know things are corny, but you know what, for those couple of times they made you jump, it was worth spending a couple bucks for a ride. Just wait for a Steam sale and get it for like a dollar like I did. This was a really well spent dollar.

[h1]👍 Highly Recommended[/h1]

[i]SIMULACRA is one of the few games that genuinely makes browsing through a smartphone feel fun. It's a horror game of sorts, but Instead of running from monsters or hiding in closets, you're piecing together the disappearance of a young woman by exploring every corner of her phone. Messages, photos, videos, emails, social media, and browser history slowly reveal a mystery that's equal parts psychological thriller and supernatural horror. It feels disturbingly believable-almost like scrolling through someone else's real device.[/i]
[hr][/hr]
[h2]🟢 PROS[/h2]
[list]
[*][b]Brilliant Found Phone Concept:[/b] Investigating an entire mystery through a lost smartphone is an incredibly immersive idea that still feels unique years after release.
[*][b]Excellent Storytelling:[/b] The narrative unfolds naturally through text messages, emails, videos, and social media instead of lengthy exposition. Every app contains another piece of the puzzle.
[*][b]Convincing Characters:[/b] Conversations feel surprisingly authentic. Friends, coworkers, and family all have believable personalities and motivations, making the investigation feel personal.
[*][b]Genuinely Creepy:[/b] SIMULACRA builds tension through unsettling discoveries, disturbing videos, and the feeling that something is deeply wrong with the phone itself.
[*][b]Creative Puzzles:[/b] Unlocking files, recovering deleted data, solving passwords, and navigating fake apps keeps the gameplay engaging throughout.
[*][b]Multiple Endings:[/b] Your decisions matter, giving the story additional replay value.
[/list]
[hr][/hr]
[h2]🔴 CONS[/h2]
[list]
[*][b]Live-Action Acting Can Be Uneven:[/b] Most performances are convincing, but a handful of scenes feel slightly awkward compared to the otherwise strong production.
[*][b]Occasional Interface Frustrations:[/b] Searching through apps or revisiting conversations can sometimes be more cumbersome than necessary.
[*][b]The Ending May Divide Players:[/b] Without spoilers, the final revelations won't satisfy everyone, especially those hoping for a more grounded explanation.
[/list]
[hr][/hr]
[h2]💰 VALUE FOR MONEY[/h2]
[b]Excellent[/b] — SIMULACRA offers several hours of engaging investigation packed with memorable moments, clever puzzles, and one of the most original horror concepts in the genre. It's frequently discounted on Steam, making it an even easier recommendation for fans of narrative adventures and psychological horror.
[hr][/hr]
[h3]⭐ 9/10[/h3]
[i]A brilliantly executed smartphone horror that proves the scariest place in a horror game isn't an abandoned mansion. Immersive, unsettling, and remarkably original, SIMULACRA remains one of the most engaging narrative horror experiences available on Steam.[/i]

[disclosure: I got this game for $1 as part of a Humble Bundle. I do think it's worth regular price though.]  

I enjoyed the story and felt they made good use of the mobile interface. It's basically a visual novel, so the story's on rails most of the time. However, there are points where your choices affect your relationships with the other characters, or where you know what to do (get in touch with someone) but not how to do it (you don't know her), so you need to get creative. 

Another nice thing about the game itself is the Begin+ feature, which speeds up the dialogue boxes on subsequent playthroughs. That'll get you through the game in about an hour instead of the usual three or four, making it a bit easier to try other paths and find all of the endings (I'm not there yet.) 

On the downside, I could have done without the pop scares. That's about as cheap as horror gets. Also, since the story and its dialogue options are all laid out for you, sometimes I had to say things I didn't believe or reveal information I wouldn't have revealed, and that hurts the immersion for me. Still, these are minor flaws in a fun, quick, entertaining game.

review_text_raw:
[h1][b] TLDR: While not noteworthy in any direction, it’s a decent low-budget mystery/thriller that is acceptable for its price. [/b] [/h1]

[h1]PROS: [/h1]
➕Good concept with phone imitation and believable features
➕Multiple decision-based endings


[h1]CONS: [/h1]
➖Severe lack of options, not even fullscreen toggle or audio options??
➖Missing some essential phone features, like ease of scrolling through tons of text messages or jumping to specific times in videos
➖Some cringe voice acting/FMV

[h1] [b] Content (Game world/Narrative) – [6/10] [/b] [/h1]
The game world takes place entirely on a phone, using the phone's UI screen. It’s a very simple imitation, but most of it works as you’d expect a phone to function. You have various apps that you go through, including email, messaging, Twitter-like  social media, photos, and dating apps. As far as a phone imitation goes, I’d say the world is fairly good, though it is missing some obvious features like being able to click on a point-in-time on a video to move to that section, or scrolling through hundreds of text messages. Otherwise, it’s good. 

The narrative focuses on a girl named Anna, who has seemingly disappeared. For some reason, Anna’s phone ends up in your possession and you have to sleuth around to figure out what happened and how to find her. 
The story has branching paths that ultimately comes down to which person you end up believing and siding with, as well as specific choices along the way that influence the ending of the game. 
I got the “Worst” ending, but was still satisfied with my playthrough because I did everything sensible and logical that I would do. To achieve the better endings, you have to do questionably moral things like [spoiler]siding with a sex offender when you have limited information[/spoiler], or [spoiler]confessing love to Anna’s best friend while pretending to be Anna.[/spoiler] In a way, it's sleazy and morally ambiguous, but I do also understand the phishing aspect of it and needing to obtain information any way possible. 
In the end, I found the story to be only “Ok” . The antagonist of a [spoiler]rogue AI[/spoiler] wasn’t very exciting or scary at the end. 

[h1][b] Gameplay (Mechanics/Difficulty) – [6/10] [/b] [/h1]
The general gameplay loop is to explore around the phone UI solving puzzles to advance the plot. 
The mechanics remind me of a watered-down version of The Rootrees Are Dead (great game, check out my review [url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/Synikx/recommended/2754380?snr=1_5_9__402]here[/url]), how you have to use hints to sleuth around a phone for information. I’d say about 70% of the puzzles in the game consist of either decoding messages or pictures, whereas the other 30% is about researching information. 
The picture/message decoding consists of either aligning pictures correctly, or putting text messages in the correct order. I found the picture puzzles to be much more challenging. The researching of information is where it’s similar to Rootrees where you need to look through emails or messages to find correct information for things like passwords. 
While the mechanics were fine, I would have much preferred the quantity of research to picture/text decoding to be reversed, that is 70% research and 30% decode. I felt like the decoding was a bit out of place. 

The difficulty is generally easy. I was stumped a few times, but the game allows a skip or nudges you in the right direction after a little bit. The only challenging part is figuring out the very specific choices to get the better endings. 

[h1] [b] Technical (Graphics/Performance) – [5/10] [/b] [/h1]
Graphics were okay. Most of the game is a phone UI, with the remaining parts being FMV or pictures. I felt that the UI looks simple, but believable. The FMV and pictures were high quality and numerous, especially in public settings, so I appreciated the realistic approach. I’d say this is around PS4-era graphics. 
Performance was flawless, zero issues. 
I do want to call out the atrocious graphical settings. I don’t think I’ve ever seen a game with less options. I think the only two are language and subtitles. Not even audio volume or full screen or resolution. 
I didn’t notice any bugs. 

1440p @ 240hz | installed on SSD  

[h1] [b] Audio – [4/10] [/b] [/h1]
There wasn’t much, if any music. 
There is ample voice acting, and half of it was super cringe. Anna did a decent job. Greg was just terrible. Taylor has ups and downs. Ashley is decent as well. 

[h1] [b] Replay Factor (Longevity) – [4/10] [/b] [/h1]
Decent replay value due to the multiple endings, but you probably need a guide for the route on how to get there. Otherwise, just achievements and easter eggs. 

[h1] [b] Final Verdict – [5/10] [/b] [/h1]
Simulacra is a horror game that takes place entirely on a phone screen, with you being the user operating the phone. This isn’t an overly terrifying game, though there is a few jump scares, and I found the plot to be okay, which is generally the linchpin with these more “Visual novel”-type games with less gameplay depth, so all things considered, it’s a fairly good game, especially for the price. 

I don’t have too many big issues with the game, just smaller ones. 
The graphical options are terrible, but thankfully, I was able to use alt+enter to play in windowed mode, since there’s no borderless option. 
I’d have liked better phone functionality, namely being able to click to any point in time for videos and ease of scrolling through dozens of text messages. Everyone has been using smartphones for decades at this point, so these basic features should be available. 
Lastly, the voice acting was pretty cringy. Cringe was generally the norm, with average performances being the exception. 

Otherwise, the gameplay through small puzzles and sleuthing, and the story, while not exceptional, were both enough to keep me interested until I hit the credits. 
There’s a lot of things that could be improved, but for the price, I think it’s a solid game worth checking out. 

[h1] [b] Recommend? (Price) [Y/N] [/b] [/h1]
[h1]Yes[/h1]
$5 is an acceptable price considering it takes around ~4 hours to beat for a single playthrough and offers multiple endings. Sale price of $1 is very good.

It's been a while since I last played "Simulacra", but since I mentioned it when reviewing "Daemon_9" I felt that it was only fair to give the game it's due. 

As with the aforementioned 'dangerous dark web' title, "Simulacra" places YOU, the player, in the lead role. Not some character. YOU. The premise is a straight-forward one: You have stumbled across some young woman's phone and, in an attempt to discover the owner's identity, you search it's contents, only to discover that the fate of that young woman, may inevitably bring upon your own undoing as well. 

As one can imagine, the very premise of this game hinges on the morally dubious premise that in attempting to find this missing girl, going by the name of Anna, players are consciously violating her privacy by accessing her personal information through her unlocked mobile device. This issue of an individual's right to privacy has been a hot topic for some time now and has been the subject of whole games in of themselves. For "Simulacra", however, this is merely a starting point and one which tells a very different story, albeit one that deals with several other equally relevant issues instead. 

The game feels far more real-world in it's dramatic critique of New Media cultures than that of "Daemon_9", exploring the far more domestic world of mobile device apps and how they can be abused by the wrong kinds of people. Essentially, the digital paper trail that players are encouraged to follow inevitably leads them into the moral grey area of dating apps and 'hook-up' culture, where along with Anna's ex-boyfriend and a somewhat dubious acquaintance of hers, they are drawn further and further into a world that is custom-gear for self-destruction through the distortion of regular human interaction. A common theme in all of these techno-phobic gaming narratives is the belief that they lead to isolation and inevitably the erasure of physical identity by way of hikikomori (feel free to Google search that word if you want to know what it means). "Simulacra" expands this idea to quite a heavy degree, causing players to interact with all manner of "influencers" and shady individuals in order to finally come face-to-face with the kidnapper.   

The trouble with this game in comparison to "Daemon_9" is that while both games involve re-playing old footage and analysing information, "Simulacra" feels like a far more passive gaming experience. Whereas the former game has characters glaring down the barrel of the camera at you, in this instance the game instead tries to maintain at least some degree of a fourth wall. Considering that the whole "Simulacra" experience concerns thrusting the player into the spotlight, this can cheapen the experience with how the player becomes immersed in the experience. Though they are facing the camera front on, actors often look off-camera when performing lines which makes it feel more like a dramatically acted close-up shot to another fictional character than a direct address to the player. Don't get me wrong. The young cast fair very well with the material that they are given and all give admirable performances. It just feels like they were being asked to treat the video sequences more like a piece of scripted drama by the director instead of recreating a piece of Vlog or V-phone footage. When all is said and done, such methods do make the overall experience a little lack-lustre given that one unnecessary degree of separation.  

More promising, however, are the dialogue phases which are conducted through SMS sequences. Here the immersion process is far more convincing, due in no small part to the fact that players are actively engaging with the drama instead of simply receiving video/audio information. The presentation of these sequences also mean that they are not hindered by the usual Stop/Start mechanics to which conversational dialogue phases are usually tied, thus making it feel more natural and organic. This immersion also helps create a sense of helplessness when control is periodically wrested away from the player in a conscious nod to the modern surge of remote hacking and cyber attacks. 

In summary, I do highly recommend "Simulacra" because it is a very good premise for a game. As Major Kusanagi famously said in the conclusion to Mamoru Oshii's "Ghost In The Shell": "The Net is vast and infinite", and as the digital landscape continues to expand the possibilities for new narrative material surrounding new media technologies grows with it. However, as a narrative gaming experience it is a mixed bag. The social commentary aspects of this game, and of it's spin-off "Simulacra: Pipe Dreams", more than warrant at least two full play throughs. However, as far as Interactive FMV dramas go, one is better suited to buying "Her Story", "The Infectious Madness of Dr. Dekker" or the "Daemon_9".

[h2] Simulacra Review: A Promising Start That Loses Its Way [/h2]

Simulacra is an intriguing, story-driven game that draws players in with its early mystery and atmosphere. However, as the game progresses, it begins to lose momentum, culminating in an abrupt and unsatisfying ending. Despite this, the game is still worth experiencing for those who enjoy narrative-focused titles, though it has a few notable shortcomings.

[h3] The Good: [/h3]

1) Compelling Start: From the beginning, Simulacra presents an engaging and mysterious premise that immediately captures the player's attention. The game’s atmosphere and pacing set the stage for an intriguing narrative.

2) Satisfying Puzzle Solving: For those with a keen eye for detail, solving the puzzles is rewarding. The game often challenges players to analyze small clues, and the sense of satisfaction upon uncovering key pieces of the story is one of its standout features.

3) Impactful Choices: The game does well in giving players the feeling that their choices matter. How you respond to certain characters affects their relationships with you, adding a layer of depth and emotional investment to the experience.

[h3] The Bad: [/h3]

1) Repetitive Gameplay: Unfortunately, the gameplay starts to feel repetitive as the game progresses. The entire experience is confined to a phone screen, and while this fits the premise, it can become tiresome over time, as the game rarely deviates from this formula.

2) Lack of Explanation for the Antagonist: The game’s main antagonist remains cryptic, with little explanation given for their motivations or origins. This leaves players with more questions than answers, which can feel frustrating for those who prefer a clear narrative.

3) Abrupt Ending: One of the biggest letdowns is the ending. For a story-based game, the conclusion should feel like a natural payoff, but instead, it feels rushed and unfinished, leaving many of the game’s intriguing threads unresolved. The game’s narrative feels carried more by its strong start than by its finale.

[h3] The Ugly: [/h3]

1) Repetitive Playthroughs: Replaying the game is a tedious process as players must start from scratch. There is no checkpoint system to revisit critical moments or alter the story’s outcome without going through the entire experience again. This makes multiple playthroughs feel like a chore.

2) Frustrating Achievements: Some of the achievements are either too obscure or require an unreasonable amount of time and patience to unlock. This might be off-putting for those who are not inclined to consult a guide or spend excessive hours grinding.

3) Annoying Sound Effects: While the sound design in Simulacra is generally effective, the game occasionally relies on loud, jarring noises in an attempt to startle the player. These moments feel cheap and detract from the otherwise immersive experience, disrupting the atmosphere rather than enhancing it.

[h3] Conclusion: 6/10 [/h3]

Simulacra has a lot to offer in terms of its mystery and narrative, especially for those who enjoy story-driven experiences. However, the lack of a satisfying ending, repetitive gameplay, and the absence of convenience features like a checkpoint system hold it back from being a truly great game. It’s definitely worth checking out if you’re a fan of mystery and story-focused titles, but if you’re sensitive to flashing lights or sudden loud noises, it might be best to approach with caution.

I must admit. I really REALLY enjoyed playing this game.

When I first saw the tag 'Horror', I was a little scared to play this. I'm not a fan of things that scare me, but I managed to get through this and had a blast. *There are a couple jumpscares obviously because why not XD* (I legit flip out at them and tell them to screw off haha)

So in short, Simulacra is about a girl named Anna who has gone missing, and you have to dig through information through her apps, photos, friends, and even people outside of her circle, in order to find out what the hell happened to her.

And I mean you have to dig through a lot of information sometimes.

However, it's not to say that it wasn't fun doing a treasure hunt. Whenever I figured out how to solve one of the tasks based on the information found in different apps, I felt overjoyed. This game makes you really look for the clues where it makes sense.

Also, by the end of the game, I almost felt like I knew the characters. They were very believable, and that's what really connected with me.

Overall, I just love the idea of using solely a phone. It creates a constraint, allowing for so many possibilities and new ways to create and solve puzzles.

I can say that I have only a couple complaints though.

1) When you look through Anna's message history, you come upon these special messages that are in complete disarray. In order to understand what it said, you had to rearrange the words to fix the message. Sometimes, it was just really difficult for me to figure out what that sentence was. I sometimes maybe spent a little too much time and couldn't progress until I figured it out. Most of the messages weren't important enough to do this, except for one. To be honest, I'm probably just not very good at it.

This review may contain light spoilers. The TL;DR is that I would recommend it, it's about 3 hours of gameplay, but is quite hand-holdy in parts. Don't go into this expecting a cerebral game where you need to figure everything out for yourself. Also, don't expect the choices the game forces you into making to make any sense, either.

I quite liked it. It's definitely an improvement from the last game, but there are a few things I noticed.
For instance, there's a few grammar and spelling mistakes in the phone's interface through the game, and most notably the 'BUSTED' chatroom, after it's just 2 people left in it, turns into 'BUSTED' is typing, as if the contact name was called 'BUSTED' and this wasn't actually a chatroom.

The knocking, gasps/breathing 'outside' the phone (This game could also be titled "Millennials don't answer the door simulator 2017") were also unneeded. It wasn't that scary and took away from the game, if you're going I was expecting a jump-scare, or some kind of mechanic where I would need to move around my house to avoid various hostile entities from 'getting me' while I solved the phone mystery. 

It was also a bit too linear and railroady for my tastes. The auto-suggestion mechanic needs a lot more work because I felt like I was constantly being railroaded in the dialogue sections down a path that there's no way I (as a person) would have done or said. I wasn't a fan of the two 'supposed-to-lose' parts, either - I spent a good half an hour on one, hunting around and going into every app and going through every bit of information I had so far trying to get more information. 

The story felt very one-track also. If you compared this game to a visual novel, which is pretty much what this game is, a standard VN player would be very dissapointed with the lack of branching paths, different dialogues, and small amount of endings.

I really want to emphasize that the 'free-roam' hunting for information was the best part of this game, and the dialogue elements forcefeeding you stuff you figured out 10 messages ago was the absolute worst. If the devs want to keep on making games like these, the dialog absolutely needs more work. Additionally it seems like the developers really wanted to characterize these people but in the process of haphazardly sprinkling photographs in there were serious inconsistences. Players are going to be combing through this stuff trying to find precious information and the last thing they need is to be misled due to a mistake.

Overall, though, I recommend a buy if this is the sort of game you like. This is a vast improvement upon the last game and I look forward to this studio's next game.

review_text_raw:
Fun game for something quite different, a bit like a detective style game using a phone interface to get to the truth.

GOOD STUFF: To me, i enjoyed it for the novelty, and there are different endings for your choices.... They have tried some unique puzzle ideas, you do have to go back and forth through lots of phone based media to solve stuff, and the game often gives you options for hints, if you want them, when stuck instead of just straight delivering them to you after 2 seconds.  They tried to capture how the current world of social media and dating can feel and added some light humour throughout the game.  if you like solving crime style puzzles with a little mystery element added on top, it is worth the short playtime for a bit of fun.

BAD STUFF: However the ridiculous immaturity/selfishness/general mood of ALL the characters had me struggling to want to side with, save or even continue to want to interact with almost any of them as the game went on... It almost makes sense, as they are around 20yrs of age, that they would be a little naive, hot headed, horny and impulsive but yeesh.... waaaaay overboard, none of them ever understand if you do anything for the safety of yourself OR them, and so much of the dialogue has an extreme teen gossip feel, omg he said that you said that she did THAAAAT guurrrrrl im not talking for 2 mins to show I hate you!!! :O haha!  
Similarly the options you can choose between often force you to move the game onwards in a way I would never even consider and would actively steer clear of if I was in this situation.... but I understand it's very difficult to set up enough paths for players to feel like they really have a choice with these things.... Still some work could be done to not feeeeeel like your responses are so forced in a certain direction.  Maybe I missed it too at the start? But suggesting your character is unable to speak or something would help make some of the game moments easier to understand/improve immersion as well.

I really appreciate what the devs have done here, and hope they continue to make some fun games with a difference to the standard algorithm stuff that floods the markets these days. It would be great if they can find a way to let characters adapt to understand the players personality and choices a little more, it's so important to games like this where you are expected to solve a crisis situation if it feels even remotely like it was your actual choices as a person that led to the consequences you get :).

OK, I have just finished one run and I would recommend it!
In shorts,

Goods:
+Lots of contents, even some random guys on Spark, very detailed characterized even for minor characters
+Climax just bumped into at the right moments
+Innovative gameplay rather than just points and clicks
+Real action characters make the game much more immersive
+There are just right amount of minigames beside pure text reading
+Spot on the mentality that people like to check on others' phones and see what're inside, eg. Gallery, videos, etc
+Low price tag!

Bads:
-I can't say Anna is poor at acting, she's good, but she's kind of zoned out during the first second of most of the clips. It looks like that she is thinking what to say then starts acting after one second
-Some unnecessary jumpscares, the script is good, the story is good, come on, you can make the atmosphere scary without cheap jumpscares, make it more subtle, eg. Anna's wallpaper is changing after certain stages, which is spooky and good
-The ending is not so good... The whole process is great but when it comes to the ending... I am ok with the setting but it would be great if the ending part was made longer
-So during the ending part, Taylor is still busy texting you when he's encountering all those shxx? That doesn't make any sense. I understand that there has to be a means to let the players know what is happening. Can't you just make it like Taylor used Facetime with you before all those happened and try to tell the story with videos? As I imagine the scene, I found it very weird that Taylor is dealing with those things and keeps looking at the phone and texts you back and forth. That would be a heavy smartphone addict...
-The story is too long but very linear, which makes replays not quite possible. I want to try the other endings, but it's harsh for me to go for another 4-hour KNOWN adventure. There are many side events to do but the main route is pretty much the same. Maybe you can make it that we start at some certain late points or make the story less linear. We don't like grinding...

That being said, it's still a very great game, I hope there are more localization subtitles coming soon that I can refer to more of my friends from other parts of the world.
I will def buy the next title from Kaigon Games!
Good job! :p

review_text_raw:
Simulacra is a found phone simulator. Apparently that's a genre now. 

On a phone, the premise of Simulacra is something special: What if your phone turned into someone else's phone, and you could hack into it to snoop out all the little things about our life that we entrust to our phones these days. And because said phone gives you complete access to the online persona of the owner of that phone, you also get to moonlight as an online predator. 

It still works well enough on the PC, although the immersion is somewhat diminished. 

But hey, it's OK, because Anna, the owner of the phone, is in trouble and you are the only one with access to enough information to maybe help her. And also…  this is just a game. 

If I sound like I'm down on the game for the icky things it expects you to do, I'm actually not. The game never shies away from pointing out how questionable the means you employ are, and if you want it, you can go about things in the most ethical way possible. You won't get the best ending, though. 

The actual means by which the game let's you morally compromise yourself are quite simple. Some light social hacking, catfishing, actual hacking, two simple mini-games. The rest of the time you read dialogue or watch a few videos with above average novice actors, and thus follow along a nifty little horror story whose ending felt very rushed but still packed quite a punch. 

The game is a bit railroady, though. The main thing you do is converse with Anna's contacts via multiple choice chat, and oftentimes the few options you have are very obviously pushing the story in the direction it wants to go. Thanks to the brevity of the game, this never gets too grating, though. 

The main freight of meaning and engagement this game transported for me was the fun and glee you can actually get out of pretending to be a terrible person with access to someone else's phone, and thinking about what that actually means for the hellscape we are all constructing for ourselves. There is no way around it: If you have no moral compass, being a troll is a very good time. Good thing then that in Simulacra, the moral justification comes with the box. 

TLDR: Interesting little title whose premise and insinuations become more horrifying the longer you think about it. Bit on the short side, but well worth experiencing.

review_text_raw:
I'm a big fan of found-phone games, and had previously enjoyed Sara Is Missing. SIMULACRA is an extension of those horror-tendrils into the tiny genre, and definitely ranks well amidst other contenders like Unrd (Last Seen Online, The Silent Truth, My Last Three Days, Now Live, etc etc), Replica, the Normal Lost Phone series, and so forth. (It should be noted that I also count alternate OS and hacking games in this genre when it allows for entrance into a character's private computer; Mainlining and Orwell definitely contribute to the genre in substantial ways--)

This one has a great narrative pushing it forward, but the big stumbling block comes from the clunky puzzle integration. Content in the phone is corrupted, and appears as fragmented photographs and jumbled up text messages that need your help in piecing back together. These broke the immersion of the game in ways that Normal Lost Phone, Unrd, and Orwell all avoided. Password puzzles were more believable, but I felt that if the developers had added something like 'download a decrypting software' or something like this, and then integrated the gamification/puzzles into that as a feature/way to pass the time, I would've received that far better than the literal piecing-together. Another issue with that was how it forcibly slowed down playthroughs on repeat-plays for the different endings. Despite these extremely minor flaws, the great acting and overall game design definitely proved to be an engaging time-eater. Websites looked and behaved believably, characters were hilarious and genuine, you found yourself caring for Anna amidst all these weirdos. I hope to see the primary antagonist's motivations and development played out over future games, as I don't believe this is the end of their story. Definite thumbs up from me.

review_text_raw:
Pretty good, truth to be told.

After receiving a mysterious phone, you quickly realize it belongs to a missing young girl, and so you start investigating over her disappearance. Using real life-like apps mimicking twitter, facebook, and Gmail (among others), you'll collect proofs, find connections and chat with the girl's acquaintances to discover an ominous truth.

The ending is a bit of a letdown, but the experience as a whole is engaging.

The game's realization did allow for some immersion and suspension of disbelief and, while there are times where as a player you are pushed in a direction you would not choose, the game flows otherwise quite nicely.

While you are investigating there are some things to do on the side: ominous messages to translate, numbers to use to unlock secret messages, etc. I don't know how many of them are around, but the one I found were a nice diversion.

Acting and voice-acting are also enjoyable most of the time: you have the impression to deal with real people and not actors, usually.

There is not much as far as audio effects are concerned, with the exception of some creepy sound ambiances in superb 3D that did actually made me jump a couple of times.

Also, the game is supposed to be replayable, there are different endings but, frankly after you find out what was all about, I don't see why one should actually do it, unless really really into the game.

All in one a pretty good game, especially for the price.

3.5/5

This is amazing work. Especially considering that it was made by a small dev team. I am an instant fan )

I believe this is the kind of game that is best to go into completely blind (don't even read the description on the store page). Part of the immersion and excitement comes from the fact that you don't know where it's going. Overall expect a good story and well written characters with some light puzzles; mechanically not very different from an adventure game. Definitely worth your time.

Light spoilers follow.

[spoiler]
What impressed me most was the way it breaks the fourth wall. Let me explain. Nowadays a lot of games engage in some kind of meta-commentary, be it lampshading or just generally making jokes or winking at the player. When it's done competently, it can be somewhat amusing.

This game does something else. It actually manages to make the player take responsibility (emotional, moral) for some of the in-game decisions. It's probably hit and miss, but there were a few moments where I was really compelled to question my judgement. Did *I* decide to do this? What does it say about me as a person? And after the game tricks you into doing something questionable, it slaps you with an achievement on top of it ) For me this was where it really shined.
[/spoiler]

review_text_raw:
Ehh....

The story is pretty silly, to be honest. I haven't gotten all of the endings but I don't really feel much desire to. I won't spoil anything but if you're into this sort of thing (Twilight Zone, Black Mirror, etc.) you probably won't be too impressed with the reveal. The game seems convinced that you care about what happens to the characters, but you aren't really given any reason to. Most of them are either rude or only play minor parts. The voice acting varies, but it's mostly pretty poor, certainly a step down after having just played Her Story. I never really felt like I was part of the game's world, since so much of what happened was out of my control and the dialog options rarely were what I actually wanted to say.

That said, there are definitely some enjoyable moments here. The music/sound is good (if a little harsh sometimes) and the visuals were better than I expected. The gameplay was pretty basic, but it was never frustrating. If the game sounds interesting to you, and you haven't already become desensitized to the genre's tropes, you'll probably feel like you got your money's worth, if not much more.
